Summary: This paper introduces ReAgent, a four-stage Detect–Fix–Retrain–Gate framework aimed at reducing structural tool-calling hallucinations (invalid tool invocations, placeholder or ungrounded arguments, and execution loops) in open-weight agents, evaluated on Aya Expanse 32B within τ²-bench (retail, airline, telecom). ReAgent combines a deterministic 12-kind Tool/Arg/Loop classifier and a companion runtime repetition monitor, oracle-verified fix generation from an open-weight teacher (GLM-5.3-Flash, selected via a 12-model bake-off), assistant-turn-masked QLoRA fine-tuning, and a pre-registered four-check development gate (DevGate). On the held-out τ²-bench test split (100 tasks × 2 samples), full-trajectory distillation (SFT v2 / Arm B) reduces Tool/Arg hallucination conversations from 95.0% to 10.0% and raises task success from 14.5% (untuned) and 13.0% (zero-shot anti-hallucination prompting) to 51.5%. The authors also compare two single-GPU healing cycles (turn-level prefix rewriting vs. full-trajectory distillation), report negative reward-hacking results for three post-SFT single-turn GRPO variants, and analyze residual post-healing failures showing a shift from structural hallucinations to policy and decision-making errors.
Strengths: High empirical transparency and statistical rigor: The paper employs strictly frozen test splits, pre-registered gating criteria, task-level paired bootstrap confidence intervals, Holm-corrected exact McNemar tests, and independent oracle re-scoring, while candidly documenting implementation bugs (e.g., SFT v4), confounds, and negative results.

Compelling safety-relevant negative results on post-SFT single-turn GRPO: The Arm H case study concretely demonstrates metric misalignment and reward hacking in write-capable agents—optimizing single-turn structural compliance rewards halves loops and lowers structural findings while inducing syntactically valid but unauthorized state mutations (e.g., 12 unrequested airline cancellations) and skipping agent-side telecom fixes.

Insightful error attribution and diagnostic findings: The analysis clearly shows that high syntactic schema validity (~98–99% on Retail/Airline) does not prevent pervasive placeholder/fabricated arguments (95% hallucination conversations), links telecom tool-call errors to function-call syntax in the support manual, and documents the post-healing bottleneck shift from structural hallucinations to domain policy and decision errors (37/55 remaining failures have zero structural findings).

Clear presentation, reproducibility, and cost-efficiency documentation: The manuscript is well-written with thorough appendices (prompts, classifier rubrics, hyperparameters, bake-off results, and verbatim transcripts) and provides concrete cost/compute accounting ($11.20 in teacher trajectories and under 30 minutes of single-H100 QLoRA training).
Weaknesses: Disconnect between the 'closed-loop self-healing' framing and the working mechanism (limited novelty): In the only configuration that substantially improves task success (full-trajectory distillation in SFT v2 / Cycle 2), the deterministic 12-kind classifier plays no role in task selection, fix synthesis, or data filtering—τ²-bench's ground-truth outcome oracle V(τ) performs those roles. Meanwhile, every classifier-driven or closed-loop component failed or did not trigger: turn-level rewriting (Cycle 1) yielded flat dev success (4/36 → 4/36), on-policy repair (SFT v4) was aborted due to bugs and API credit exhaustion, structural GRPO degraded accuracy, DevGate Check 3 never rejected a candidate, and the live runtime monitor fired 0 times. Furthermore, 'autonomous' Cycle 2 relied on SFT v2's manually augmented, dev-informed pool (34 extra airline trajectories added after SFT v1 failed DevGate). Consequently, the working core reduces largely to standard offline oracle-verified teacher-trajectory QLoRA distillation combined with manual domain upsampling and a dev non-regression gate.

Narrow scope and weak practical motivation: All healing experiments test a single weak baseline student (Aya Expanse 32B, 14.5% untuned) on a single English customer-service benchmark (τ²-bench, 100 test tasks). Comparable or smaller open-weight models in the authors' own bake-off (e.g., Qwen3.8 27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma 4 31B) substantially outperform even the healed Aya model zero-shot. Neither a stronger student, a second benchmark, multilingual performance, nor general-capability retention is evaluated to justify adapting Aya or demonstrate broader generalization.

Severely confounded comparison between turn-level and trajectory-level healing (Cycle 1 vs. Cycle 2): The two cycles simultaneously vary fix granularity, task pool size (30 vs. 112), per-lesson deduplication (16 turns / 938 target tokens vs. 136 full conversations), batch size, training steps (16 vs. 68), and manual airline upsampling, making it impossible to isolate the causal effect of turn-level vs. trajectory-level supervision.

Avoidable serving confounds, incomplete ablations, and missing inference-time baselines: (a) On the primary Test table (Table 2), Arms A and C run on Cohere's hosted API (128K context) while Arm B runs locally on vLLM (32K context, causing 2/200 overflows and confounding latency), even though matched self-hosted control Arm P already existed and was run on Dev/Val; (b) step-matched ablation SL (112 trajectories, 74 steps) was not evaluated on Dev, leaving it unresolved whether SFT v2's DevGate promotion came from the 34 extra airline trajectories or simply from 74 vs. 56 training steps; and (c) only zero-shot prompting (Arm C) is evaluated as a baseline on Test, omitting stronger zero-weight-update baselines such as pre-execution interception/retry using the authors' own deterministic classifier, grammar/schema-constrained decoding in vLLM, and few-shot prompting.

Biased, outcome-conditioned Validation split: Constructing the 30-task Validation set as the exact complement of the 112 healable train tasks (15 tasks already solved by base Aya plus 15 tasks where the teacher failed) introduces strong selection bias across all Table 4 ablations and leaves only 5 airline tasks.

Incomplete classifier validation and weak auxiliary evidence: Classifier precision was spot-checked on only 30 telecom failures under an earlier handoff rule; retail and airline precision and overall recall were never measured, and 3 of the 12 error kinds never appeared in the spot check. In addition, GRPO Arm G's collapse stems largely from a dataset-construction artifact (training solely on tool-call turns without reply turns), and SFT v4's incomplete run leaves on-policy failure-point SFT unassessed.
Questions: Why was the matched self-hosted control (Arm P on local vLLM) not evaluated on the 100-task Test split to eliminate the Cohere API (128K) vs. vLLM (32K) serving confound in Table 2?

What is the Dev performance (including per-domain Retail/Airline/Telecom pass counts) of the step-matched ablation SL (112 trajectories, 74 steps), and does it pass DevGate without the 34 extra airline trajectories?

How does weight-level SFT compare against inference-time structural guardrails—specifically, deploying the deterministic 12-kind classifier C as a pre-execution interceptor that returns corrective feedback for retry, or enabling constrained decoding in vLLM?

In an unconfounded comparison between turn-level prefix rewriting and full-trajectory distillation (matched on the 112-task pool, without per-lesson deduplication, and matched on token budget or gradient steps—or run across multiple sequential cycles), does turn-level supervision still fail to improve task success?

How would a genuinely autonomous multi-cycle loop detect and remediate domain regressions (such as Airline in SFT v1) without manual human inspection and injection of the 34 dev-informed airline trajectories, and why did Cycle 2 train on 136 conversations compared to 146 in SFT v2?
Does ReAgent generalize to a stronger open-weight student or a second benchmark, and does English-only τ²-bench QLoRA fine-tuning degrade Aya Expanse 32B's multilingual or general capabilities?
Can you report precision and recall of the 12-kind classifier across all three domains (including exact heuristics for the `ungrounded` argument detector)?
Limitations: The authors transparently discuss six core limitations in the manuscript (single weak student/benchmark/language, policy-decision ceiling, teacher and oracle dependency, co-varying Cycle 1/2 factors and dev-informed Cycle 2 pool, serving confounds and missing capability-retention checks, and partial classifier validation).

Additional methodological limitations include the outcome-conditioned construction of the 30-task Validation split (biasing Table 4 model-selection comparisons), low statistical power of small per-domain dev slices (e.g., 6 airline tasks) for automated regression gating, and the reliance on sandboxed simulated users and automated terminal-state oracles V(τ) that are generally unavailable in live production logs.

Potential negative societal impact: Deploying write-capable tool-calling agents in customer-service settings carries real consumer-harm risks (such as unauthorized cancellations or refunds, as illustrated by GRPO Arm H); over-reliance on automated structural metrics or synthetic staging oracles could mask subtle policy or intent violations in production.
